title: Bag of Tricks for Efficient Text Classification
summary: Deep neural network text classifiers are accurate but slow to train and evaluate, limiting their use on very large datasets. The paper proposes fastText, a linear classifier with a rank constraint: word (and hashed n-gram) embeddings are averaged into a hidden text representation and fed to a softmax layer (hierarchical softmax for large output spaces), trained with asynchronous SGD and a linearly decaying learning rate. fastText matches or beats deep models such as char-CNN and is close to VDCNN on 8 sentiment benchmarks (e.g., 92.5% on AG News with bigrams) while training orders of magnitude faster (1s per epoch on AG News; over one billion words in under ten minutes on a multicore CPU) and reaches 46.1 prec@1 on YFCC100M tag prediction in minutes.

match_target.why: Honours the user's hint. It is the flagship row of Table 1 (the paper's central 'on par with deep learning' result: 92.5% vs 92.4 for ngrams-TFIDF and 87.2 for char-CNN), yet by far the cheapest to reproduce: AG News is small (120k train), needs no pretrained embeddings, and trains in seconds on a CPU per Table 2, so the full lr grid costs only minutes.

tolerance.why: Rule 2: the paper reports no std over repeated runs; the metric is test accuracy in % and the AG News test split in the Zhang et al. (2015) protocol contains 7,600 examples (>2,000), so the band is +/-1.0 absolute point.

requirements.stmt: Implement the rank-constrained linear model of Figure 1: an embedding look-up matrix A, whose rows for the input features are averaged into a hidden text representation of dimension h, fed to a linear classifier B.
requirements.quote: The word representations are then averaged into a text representation, which is in turn fed to a linear classifier.

requirements.stmt: Train by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of the labels under a softmax over the predefined classes.
requirements.quote: We use the softmax function f to compute the probability distribution over the predefined classes.

requirements.stmt: Each document input xn is the normalized bag of its features (words plus, optionally, n-grams).
Optimize with asynchronous stochastic gradient descent on multiple CPU threads and a linearly decaying learning rate.
requirements.quote: This model is trained asynchronously on multiple CPUs using stochastic gradient descent and a linearly decaying learning rate.

requirements.stmt: For the bigram variant, add n-grams as extra features mapped with the hashing trick (same hash function as Mikolov et al. 2011) into 10M bins when only bigrams are used.
requirements.quote: with the same hashing function as in Mikolov et al. (2011) and 10M bins if we only used bigrams, and 100M otherwise

requirements.stmt: For the Table 1 sentiment experiments use exactly 10 hidden units, 5 training epochs, and select the learning rate on a validation set from {0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5}.
requirements.quote: We use 10 hidden units and run fastText for 5 epochs

requirements.stmt: Evaluate on the same 8 datasets (AG, Sogou, DBPedia, Yelp Polarity/Full, Yahoo! Answers, Amazon Full/Polarity) with the same evaluation protocol as Zhang et al. (2015).
requirements.quote: We employ the same 8 datasets and evaluation protocol of Zhang et al. (2015).

requirements.stmt: Keep the architecture parameters identical across all 8 datasets (single configuration per row of Table 1, with and without bigrams).
requirements.quote: FastText has been run with the same parameters for all the datasets.

requirements.stmt: Train all embeddings from scratch on the classification task; do not use any pre-trained word vectors.
requirements.quote: Unlike Tang et al. (2015), fastText does not use pre-trained word embeddings

requirements.stmt: For large output spaces (tag prediction), replace the full softmax by hierarchical softmax based on a Huffman coding tree to get O(h log2(k)) training complexity.
requirements.quote: we use a hierarchical softmax (Goodman, 2001) based on the Huffman coding tree (Mikolov et al., 2013)

requirements.stmt: Use the bag of n-grams only as additional features capturing partial local word order; word order is not modeled explicitly.
requirements.quote: we use a bag of n-grams as additional features to capture some partial information about the local word order

data.name: AG News (Zhang et al. 2015 CSV: 120,000 train / 7,600 test, 4 classes)
data.how_to_get: CSV release from Zhang et al. (2015); widely mirrored, e.g. https://s3.amazonaws.com/fast-ai-nlp/ag_news_csv.tgz (fast.ai mirror of the Zhang et al. CSV) or the CharCnn_Keras GitHub data folder.

data.name: Full 8-dataset bundle of Zhang et al. (2015): AG, Sogou, DBPedia, Yelp Review Polarity/Full, Yahoo! Answers, Amazon Review Full/Polarity
data.how_to_get: CSV mirrors on GitHub (e.g., the 'data' folder of mhjabreel/CharCnn_Keras) and various Kaggle re-uploads; only needed for claims C2-C6.

data.name: YFCC100M metadata (for the tag-prediction claim C7 only)
data.how_to_get: Yahoo Webscope YFCC100M release (Thomee et al., 2016); the paper states 'We will release a script that recreates this dataset' — not required for the match target.

stated_compute: Both char-CNN and VDCNN are trained on a NVIDIA Tesla K40 GPU, while our models are trained on a CPU using 20 threads.
